text: I think it mostly comes down to planetary protection. Cassini had spent years flying around Saturn and past its moons, so it was covered in a lot of unknown stuff, and nobody wanted it drifting into Enceladus or Titan by accident. Those moons are interesting because they might be good candidates for finding life, so keeping them clean matters. Crashing into Saturn's atmosphere meant destroying the probe in the gas giant itself, far from the moons. It was a deliberate choice to make sure the spacecraft wouldn't contaminate places scientists later want to study.

Honestly, if you're spending a lot of time braking or dragging a foot, that stationary leg is doing all the heavy lifting. I think what's happening is that your body has to fight gravity and deceleration forces while one foot is locked to the ground. Your leg isn't just holding your weight, it's acting as the primary shock absorber for the whole board. The muscles in the quad and glutes are working overtime to keep you from tipping over. And because skateboarding on pavement means dealing with constant micro-impacts, that locked leg is taking all the jarring vibrations right down into the joints.

It's kind of wild when you think about it. You're basically doing isometric holds combined with impact absorption, and your body isn't naturally wired to hold one leg rigidly for extended periods. I've seen a lot of people get sore here simply because their technique leaves them with one foot acting as a brake for miles. The stationary leg has to stabilize the center of mass, which puts a weird rotational torque on the hip and knee. I'd check if your foot is dragging at a good angle. A lot of the pain comes from dragging too flat or pulling the board too hard, which overworks the calves and shins. The shock from hitting a crack or a pothole travels straight up the locked leg, which is why you feel it deep in the muscle rather than just the bone.

So my guess is you need to alternate your stance more often, or just ease up on the foot braking. You can also try shifting your weight back a bit to take the pressure off that specific leg. If you keep doing the exact same thing, that one leg is going to pay the price for all the deceleration. I'm pretty sure a quick stretch after you finish riding will help the tired quads and hamstrings recover, but changing how you brake is the real fix for the pain you're feeling.

Short answer: "Afro-American" doesn't mean the person is from Africa now. It's a heritage label. Most Black people in the US aren't from Africa in the way that suggests they just moved there. They're American, often with families in the US for centuries, but the ancestry usually traces back to the African continent. That's the part the word "Afro" is pointing to.

Honestly, I think it's also just a convenient category. There's a broad range of African origins within the group, and not everyone identifies the same way. The term is used when you want to acknowledge that shared background without needing to prove where each person is from. So it's less about "from Africa" in the everyday sense and more about where the lineage comes from. You can be an American in all the ways that matter while still being called Afro-American because of that ancestral connection. It's kind of like calling someone with Italian heritage "Italian-American" even if their family has lived in the US for generations. It's a heritage descriptor, not a passport stamp.

Honestly, the idea that a drug can give you the good stuff and nothing else is a bit of a fantasy. The same receptor activity that creates euphoria also creates dependence and side effects, and your body doesn't let you pick only one. If a substance lights up the reward system strongly enough, the brain starts recalibrating. Tolerance builds, cravings show up, and that's already a side effect even if no one's crashing from a withdrawal.

Most of the common "bad" stuff isn't bad because of some mystical impurity. It's bad because intense pleasure is a loud signal and the nervous system takes it seriously. Opioids bind to specific receptors and change how pain and mood are processed, stimulants crank up dopamine and norepinephrine, and that's why they can make you feel great while also making you restless, hungry, or wired. You can't isolate the pleasure part without also dragging along the physiological costs.

So can there be a drug with zero adverse effects? In principle, maybe. In practice, almost every compound strong enough to produce intense euphoria will do something else too. It's like asking for a coffee with caffeine but none of the other compounds. You get the energy without the jitters, but the whole reason caffeine works is because it messes with adenosine, and that's exactly what you don't want it to do. The pleasure and the side effects share the same doorway.

There is a small niche of experimental or newly identified compounds, but even those are usually still being studied, and the "zero effects" claim is usually relative, not absolute. What counts as "zero" for one person might be a problem for another. Tolerance, withdrawal, changes in sleep, mood swings, and appetite changes are all common, and those don't always make headlines but they're still adverse effects.

One minor thing people miss: the dose matters a lot. A drug that's gentle at a low dose can be rough at a higher one, and the line between a pleasurable experience and an adverse reaction isn't a fixed point. My guess is that the question assumes a binary where the drug is either useful or harmful, but most substances sit on a spectrum.

So why are all drugs "bad"? Mostly because "bad" is doing a lot of work in that word. The real answer is that pleasure and harm usually travel together, not because someone decided drugs should have costs, but because the mechanisms that produce the good feelings are the same mechanisms that cause the bad ones. And no, not every drug is bad in the same way, but I'm pretty sure none are completely free of tradeoffs. That's why I'd be skeptical of anything claiming zero adverse effects.

Hey there,

Honestly, that sounds less like a headache and more like your body complaining about a long, tiring day. You're probably on your feet, walking a lot, carrying bags, and dealing with crowds and decisions, so the "pain" may just be muscle fatigue, stress, and exhaustion adding up.

I'd bet it's very real and not in your head. I'd also consider whether you're dehydrated, under-slept, or gripping your jaw or shoulders tight. If it keeps happening, keep a small log of what you were doing and how you felt, and mention it to a doctor.

Take care of yourself,  
Sam

Hey,

Ha, that sounds like a pretty classic memory slip. You didn’t actually “think” milk was right. Your brain latched onto the cow and milk connection so tightly that when the question was asked, that association just fired first. It’s one of those moments where the familiar word wins over the correct one.

Honestly, that doesn’t mean you forgot the real answer. It’s just that the “cow = milk” link is stronger in memory than the “cow drinks water” link, so the stronger one popped out. If it’s only happening occasionally, it’s normal. If you’re noticing it a lot, it’s worth keeping an eye on, but it doesn’t automatically mean anything serious.

Take care,
[Your Name]

Hi Sam,

You wrote “a few questions on house-buying stuff,” so I’ll assume you mean the practical stuff, not the fairy-tale version of it. Honestly the big thing is financing, and I’d start there before you even look at houses. Get pre-approval, get the real number, then shop within that number. That saves you from falling for the pretty kitchen and ending up paying mortgage for a home you can barely afford.

I think the most interesting part is all the small stuff nobody warns you about: inspection, surveys, and title checks. I’m pretty sure those are where the hidden problems show up, and you want them done before you commit. It’s kind of wild how much can go wrong behind a painted-over wall.

You’ll want a solicitor, but don’t overthink the lawyers; most are okay, you just want someone responsive. Also check local taxes and any covenants before you settle, because those surprise people later.

I’d ask for a mortgage pre-approval letter, then walk through the inspection with an expert.

Talk soon,
M

Hey Sam,

Honestly the big difference is what you're asking the formula to do at once. A normal bodywash is built to clean skin, so it's loaded with surfactants and usually smells nice, but it isn't trying to condition hair. A 2-in-1 shampoo/conditioner is basically hair only, with enough cleansing agents plus some conditioning agents mixed in so hair feels softer after rinsing. A 3-in-1 has to walk a narrower path. It has to remove skin oils and dirt, but it also has to leave a lubricating, softening film on hair. That usually means milder surfactant choices, more emollients and conditioning agents, and a formulation that won't make skin feel tight or hair feel straw-like. In practice, I think you'll notice it's often slightly more expensive, and the tradeoff is that none of the three jobs is as strong as a dedicated product. For skin, it's gentler; for hair, the conditioning is lighter. And that's the tradeoff. You get convenience, not peak performance. If your hair's pretty healthy and your skin isn't super dry, it's usually fine for a quick wash. But if you're dealing with very dry skin or damaged hair, I'd still use separate products. So the real answer is balance, not a magic extra ingredient.

Cheers,
Alex

Hi Maya,

Nice question. The short version is that they don't usually track a whole continent as one solid block. They measure how individual points on the ground are moving relative to a reference frame, and then piece that together into plate motion.

The main tool these days is GPS. Permanently installed geodetic stations are placed on stable bedrock, and over months or years their positions are tracked with very high precision. The tiny year-to-year shifts are averaged out and turned into velocity vectors. That's how you get statements like "North America is moving a couple of centimeters per year in a given direction."

There are also space-based methods. VLBI uses radio telescopes tracking distant quasars, and satellite techniques like InSAR can show deformation over wider areas. Those help check and refine the GPS-derived velocities, especially across big tectonic boundaries.

The tricky bit is reference. Movement has to be described relative to some frame, like a fixed Earth coordinate system, not just "moving left." So the numbers are relative, and different frames can give slightly different values.

It's kind of wild that the whole idea rests on tiny annual shifts being measurable. I'd be surprised if you could feel or see it at the ground level, but the instruments can.

Best,
Sam

Mostly it's about hiding harmful recessive variants. When two people share close relatives, they're more likely to carry the same rare mutations. If both pass the same faulty gene to a child, the child ends up with two bad copies, which can show up as lower IQ. As far as I know this is a probabilistic effect: inbreeding doesn't always produce lower scores, it just raises the chance that a child inherits two copies of the same rare variant.

It's also worth noting that IQ isn't caused by one gene, so the effect depends on which combinations land in the offspring. The science is really about increased homozygosity, which is a bit of jargon, but the practical point is simple: shared ancestry means overlapping genetic mistakes.

Short answer: it's mostly about where the nerves are and how densely packed they are. The arm has softer tissue and fewer nerve endings than, say, your hands, feet, or face, so the same kind of injury often feels less intense there.

I've noticed that a cut in the upper arm really doesn't feel as sharp as a cut in the fingers, and I think that tracks with the arm being less "busy" with nerves. It's not that the arm is numb, it's just that other spots have far more pain-sensitive areas. So if you're comparing a stab in the upper arm to one in the hand, the arm tends to hurt less, and that's pretty much down to the local nerve density and tissue makeup.

Short answer: carbon monoxide actively steals the spots in your blood that oxygen needs, whereas carbon dioxide is just a waste product your body is built to clear.

Your blood carries oxygen on tiny proteins called hemoglobin. Carbon monoxide grabs onto these proteins about 200 times tighter than oxygen does. Once it sits there, it blocks oxygen from getting into your tissues. Your brain and organs start starving for air, which is why it's so deadly. You might feel like you have a bad headache or dizziness, but you don't realize your blood is suffocating your cells. It's a very sneaky way to lose oxygen.

Carbon dioxide is different. Your body makes it constantly as a byproduct of basic metabolism. You can breathe in higher amounts of CO2 and your brain will just tell your lungs to breathe faster to get rid of it. It doesn't latch onto hemoglobin like CO does. So while a very high concentration of CO2 can suffocate you by pushing oxygen out of the air mix, at everyday levels it's just something you exhale. To be fair, CO2 isn't harmless if the room is completely sealed. But in normal conditions, your body handles it easily. CO is the real threat because your body can't easily shake it off once it's bound. When you're breathing in a closed space, the CO builds up fast. You can't smell it coming, and by the time you feel dizzy, a lot of your hemoglobin is already blocked. It's a weird trap, and I'd be careful if you're ever in a poorly ventilated space with a combustion engine or gas heater.

So the brace position is a set of movements you make in your seat before a hard impact. You plant your feet, bend your knees, keep your back against the seat, and either cross your arms or place your hands over the back of the seat. It sounds small, but the point is to stop your body from moving around. In a crash, the aircraft stops suddenly and you keep going until something stops you. Bracing is about controlling where you hit and how much you move.

This matters most at low altitude, where there isn't enough time for full evasive maneuvers. It isn't a magic fix, and it doesn't remove all risk. But compared with not bracing, it reduces the chance of your head snapping back into the seatback or your limbs knocking into cabin surfaces. The technique takes practice to do quickly and naturally, which is why it's worth learning before you need it.

Short answer: we don't really remember companies the same way we remember modern brands. Before factories, mass media, and global shipping, most firms were local, or they were trading houses, guilds, and merchant families that were famous to the people they traded with. A business could be important and even respected, but that doesn't mean it's famous to us today. Well-known brand recognition needs the machinery of the industrial era: mass production, standardization, advertising, and distribution that can reach a huge audience. That's why the names that stick in our heads are usually from after those systems became common.

I keep seeing dealer ads promising the lowest APR in the county, and I get why people trust that pitch. But when I actually sat down and compared offers, the bank usually came out cheaper, and the reason is pretty simple. A lower interest rate on the loan doesn't mean the total cost is lower. The dealership makes money in the parts you don't see unless you ask. They can sell you an extended warranty, a service package, paint protection, a tire-and-battery package, and a “gap” insurance policy, and those things can add thousands of dollars to the price of the car. The loan then gets calculated on a higher amount, so even a lower rate doesn't save you money if the base price has quietly gone up.

My position is this: the bank is the safer choice unless you force the dealer to strip out every add-on and price match the bank's loan terms. Banks price loans more straightforwardly, and the number they quote is usually the whole story. A dealer will quote you the lowest rate to win the deal, then build the cost into the vehicle price or the loan amount. That's not a conspiracy, it's just how dealer financing works. You're paying for their overhead, sales incentives, and the dealer's preferred lender margin.

The detail that catches a lot of people is the payoff math. If the dealer raises the price by $2,000 to fund their own profit, your loan is bigger. A 4% rate on a bigger loan can easily cost more than a 5% rate on a smaller loan. I've seen this flip in real quotes. The bank offer had a slightly higher rate, but the total paid off over the term was lower because the loan amount was smaller. In other words, rate alone doesn't tell you which deal is better. You have to compare the total amount you'll actually repay.

So if you're shopping, ask the dealer to show you the itemized breakdown before you commit, and ask for the add-ons to be removed. Then take the bank's number side by side and compare total repayment. Most of the time, the bank wins because there's less room to hide costs.

Honestly, the state-by-state patchwork for marijuana legality is a mess. I think that's actually good. Colorado went first with recreational use in 2012, and California followed for adults in 2018. What I find interesting is how each state gets to experiment with its own rules. Some states are still strictly medical, some are fully legal, and a few still treat it like a crime. I don't love the confusion, but I also don't think the federal government is ready to solve it. States get to figure out taxes, licenses, and age limits on their own, and that's useful. It's not a perfect system, but it's real. I'd like to see one coherent national rule, but I understand why it's messy.

My take is that the body doesn’t store electricity the way a battery does. It makes it on demand, by shuffling ions across cell membranes. In a neuron, sodium ions rush in and potassium ions get pushed out, and that rapid charge movement is the electrical signal that fires down the nerve. The heart works the same way, but with its own built-in rhythm: the sinoatrial node starts the cycle and the impulse spreads across the muscle. That’s why a healthy heart needs no external trigger. The interesting part isn’t the spark itself, but the fact that this happens billions of times, quietly, without you ever having to think about it.

I still remember the first time I properly understood what sampling actually is. For years I thought it was just cutting a snippet out of an old record and dropping it under a new track, like a little borrowed heartbeat. The reality is much messier and honestly more fun. Musicians don’t usually take a clean chunk from a master recording; they’re often digging through crates, finding a 7-inch single, a B-side, or a live cut, and isolating a few seconds that have a specific rhythmic or melodic quality.

My position is that sampling is the most practical—and in its best examples, the most respectful—way to keep older music alive. When done carefully, it isn’t theft; it’s collaboration across decades. A producer might take a three-second piano figure, slow it down, pitch it a fifth lower, and build a whole beat around the new texture. That short gesture turns a forgotten recording into the foundation of something new, while the original song gains a second life. That second life is what matters to me. It’s not just nostalgia; it’s a way of saying this bit of music was worth saving and was worth reshaping.

There’s a lot of craft in the chopping. You can slice a groove into sixteenth-note stabs, rearrange the order, or overlay the passage over itself to thicken it. The detail that surprises people is how little audio sometimes has to match: a two-second break beat can anchor an entire chorus. That’s why sampling feels less like copying and more like editing. You’re selecting, not reproducing.

I also think the legal side matters, but I won’t turn this into a lecture. In practice, most sample-based hits either clear rights or stay in a grey zone where both the composer/label and the new artist benefit. The interesting part is the creative conversation it starts: one person’s old record becomes another person’s starting point, and the lineage of a song becomes a web rather than a straight line.

What gets me every time is the human element. You can trace a modern beat back through layers of older recordings, each one adding its own fingerprint. That’s not a defect; it’s the point. Sampling lets musicians talk to the past instead of merely echoing it.

I've thought about this more than once. The brain itself doesn't have pain receptors, so your actual brain can't feel the pain. What hurts are the blood vessels and the membranes around it, called the meninges. When a headache hits, those vessels and tissues swell, stretch, and release chemical signals that trigger pain. Tension headaches come from neck and scalp muscles tightening up. Migraines are a bit different and involve waves of nerve activity. So when you ask why your head hurts, the honest answer is: it's not your thoughts or memories that are hurting. It's the plumbing and the scaffolding. And yes, the pounding you feel is often blood flow changes. It's not mystical; it's mostly pressure and irritation on things that actually can feel pain.

We couldn’t judge the food, since we never actually got to eat. Showed up at 7:20 p.m. on Sunday. Picked this place because we had a 10:00 p.m. show at the same hotel, and figured it’d be an easy night. We added our names to their digital waitlist, which is honestly useless, and were told to come back at 8:23 p.m. to pay. We did, then stood around until 8:40 p.m. before staff casually dropped that we probably wouldn’t be seated until 9:15 p.m. Just the two of us, and they offered zero solutions. If the wait stretches that far past payment, just say it upfront so people don’t waste the whole evening. Honestly, absolute disaster. Zero stars if that were an option.

I went to this buffet on a Friday around 4:30 p.m., and surprisingly there wasn't a line at all. Two people came out to about $130, which felt pretty steep. Before going, I had figured the price would be comparable to a steakhouse, but afterward I learned it actually cost a bit more than I'd expected.

Honestly, I was disappointed that there was no steak. At that price, I assumed there'd be some kind of steak option. The meats were lamb, prime rib, and chicken, but those are things you can find at other Las Vegas buffets for far less money.

The seafood station had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaskan legs show up in a lot of Vegas buffets, but I hadn't run into rock crab claws anywhere else, so that was the interesting part. The problem was no crab-claw crackers. Staff said wooden mallets were available, but our table was so close to the next one that I didn't want to start smashing shells and send pieces flying at the people next to us. So I just ate the legs.

The Asian station didn't seem especially distinctive; it reminded me a lot of the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert had gelato and pastries, but nothing really stood out. They also had fresh juices, though I didn't try any.

Overall I'd call this buffet acceptable but overpriced for what it offers. If you're curious, it's worth trying once, especially if there's no wait. If the line is long, I'd probably reconsider.

★★★★☆ Keeping it

The space bar rattles. Hit it with the edge of your thumb and it sounds like a loose pen cap in a drawer. The E key also repeats now and then, so "example" becomes "eexample" and I have to backspace. It happens maybe once an afternoon, always when I'm typing fast and not looking.

I paid $38 and kept it anyway, because of the switches. When I asked the seller what they were, the answer took a week. By then I had already pulled off a keycap and found out for myself: brown tactile switches, with a small bump under the finger and a soft landing at the bottom. My old membrane board felt like pressing wet cardboard by comparison.

My job is mostly email, often two or three hours in a row, and my wrists don't ache by the end anymore. That mattered more than the rattle.

Sending it back would have meant paying for postage and boxing it up, and I'd have been without a keyboard while I waited. So it stays on the desk, and I tap the space bar a little closer to the middle now.

I’ve been going to Vegas pretty much my whole life—well, the under-21 version of it—so I’ve sat through a lot of shows before I could even gamble. Le Rêve at the Wynn is one I finally caught, and honestly? Mixed. Maybe slightly worse than mixed.

The circular stage is genuinely smart. You’re basically looking down into it, so from essentially any seat you get a decent view, which is rare in Vegas. A few individual acts are impressive too—the strength stuff, the aerialists, the divers. Those people are athletes, no question. But a lot of it reminded me of Cirque du Soleil. Not in a “rip-off” way exactly, just… if you’ve seen Cirque, you’ve seen comparable feats done with maybe more clarity.

And clarity is the problem. What is the story? I still don’t know. There’s a dream, maybe? A guy? Water? It felt like a bunch of pretty images thrown at you, and the show never tells you what it’s trying to say. Also, there’s way too much happening at once. Too many people, too many elements, too many “wow” moments stacked on top of each other. A more restrained production would hit harder. This felt like the stereotypical Vegas spectacle thing—more must be better—so they crammed everything in.

Ticket note: if you’re staying at Wynn or Encore, they have a deal—$99 instead of the normal $125. That helps. Would I see it again? Probably not, and I wouldn’t pay for it a second time. Apart from a few stunts, it was just average. I wasn’t blown away, and I don’t think anyone else was either. That said, a few friends liked it, and if you’ve never seen it, maybe check it out. Just don’t expect to leave overwhelmed.

Two years ago I ordered two shirts for my dad from Rockmount Ranch Wear over the phone. What happened next is a bit embarrassing: the rep’s handwritten 7 looked like a 1, so instead of sending the package to 5407, it went to 5401. The people there took it to the local UPS store for return, but after that the package disappeared and never showed up again. We only found out several weeks later. During the dispute, I put in another order for two shirts, but Rockmount refused to refund the original pair. The owner handled the case and admitted the shipment had gone to the wrong address, yet he said no refund unless the shirts were returned. He even suggested we were partly responsible for not being friendly enough to the residents at 5401, just four doors away. I disputed the original charge with our card company and, after some back-and-forth, we eventually got a credit.
